[PSI-20 ACME BRE] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous (emulating condensed/solid fuels) | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME
Section: objectives
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties.
The specific flight objectives are as follows.
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)
text:
[PSI-20 ACME BRE] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous (emulating condensed/solid fuels) | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME
Section: approach
To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed. Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests. For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure. Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition. The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate. Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test. As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map. Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached. At this time the fuel flow will be terminated. So a test should terminate for a given flow rate at extinction, and for continued burning when the burner surface temperature has steadied or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor is neared. The extinction limit could be found once the burner temperature has steadied, and the heat flux sensor has not exceeded its limit. At that state, the flow rate can be reduced in small increments, until extinction is observed and the flow rate shut off. Again, in this process, new data is being produced for the flammability map. Ignition limit tests are not proposed for microgravity, but we will explore these under normal gravity. We believe there is better control on Earth-based ignition testing and that these results should carry over to microgravity conditions.

Section: approach (2)
In addition to the flight experiments, in normal gravity testing will continue. These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels. These experiments will further establish the validation of the BRE for 1-g applications and show its usefulness to establish 1-g ignition and extinction limits. As available, drop facility testing will be used to refine procedures, test instrumentation, and help to establish viable flow conditions. We will also pursue a CFD model for the quiescent microgravity burning. This will also guide us in the flight experiments, and potentially provide a predictive methodology.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)
text:
[PSI-20 ACME BRE] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous (emulating condensed/solid fuels) | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME
Section: hypothesis
The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties. Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible. The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment. It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point. This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials.

The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix). Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE)
text:
[PSI-20 ACME BRE] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator (ACME BRE) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous (emulating condensed/solid fuels) | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME
Section: research impacts / earth benefits
BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

text:
[PSI-25 BASS-II] Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid | hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
Section: objectives
BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. Objectives Include: 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. 3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements. 4) Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections. The primary variables include: Forced flow velocity (speed and direction); Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation); Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets).

title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II)
text:
[PSI-25 BASS-II] Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid | hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
Section: approach
Microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time 'lab partner' operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.

title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II)
text:
[PSI-25 BASS-II] Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid | hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
Section: hypothesis
BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material.

title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II)
text:
[PSI-25 BASS-II] Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid | hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
Section: research impacts / earth benefits
A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you're on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

text:
[PSI-26 BASS] Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid | hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
Section: objectives
The two main objectives for BASS are to: 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible). 2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.

title: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)
text:
[PSI-26 BASS] Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid | hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
Section: approach
The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage) igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction. This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread. Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric. Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.

Section: hypothesis
BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.

title: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)
text:
[PSI-26 BASS] Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid | hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)
Section: research impacts / earth benefits
Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques. BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

text:
[PSI-69 FLEX] Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: liquid droplets | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) - Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
Section: objectives
The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations.

title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) - Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF)
text:
[PSI-69 FLEX] Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: liquid droplets | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) - Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
Section: approach
The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI. Procedure: 1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests. 2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm). 3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion. 4. Perform a droplet combustion test. 5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed). 6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction). 7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction. 8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite. Where extinction droplet sizes were too small to observe, the LOI was found iteratively (burn to completion followed by a no-ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in oxygen mole fraction. In slow-flow tests, near the end of burning the droplet is subjected to a small, sub-buoyant convective flow (by translating the droplet at a slow uniform speed) to see how this flow influences extinction. Many tests involve free (unsupported) droplets, some with a slow drift velocity.

Section: hypothesis
The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions.

Section: research impacts / earth benefits
Improved fire safety protocols for future space missions where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, insights can advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. Findings on the effectiveness of suppressants (CO2, He, SF6) in microgravity can lead to more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts. The study of 'cool flames' and low-temperature combustion observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines with improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions.

title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I)
text:
[PSI-98 SAFFIRE-I] Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid (large scale) | hardware: Saffire 1 enclosure in Cygnus
Section: approach
The Saffire-1 experiment was performed on the Orbital Science's Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction, and two anemometers tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked.

title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I)
text:
[PSI-98 SAFFIRE-I] Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid (large scale) | hardware: Saffire 1 enclosure in Cygnus
Section: hypothesis
This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.

title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I)
text:
[PSI-98 SAFFIRE-I] Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: solid (large scale) | hardware: Saffire 1 enclosure in Cygnus
Section: research impacts / earth benefits
The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA's material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

Section: objectives
Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. text:

Section: approach
SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house at GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16 to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post-flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.

title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
text:
[PSI-102 SAME] Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: smoke / pyrolysis (overheated materials) | hardware: Comparative Soot Diagnostic hardware, Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), thermophoretic samplers, two smoke detectors (ionization + photoelectric/DustTrak)
Section: approach
The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined. The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.

Section: hypothesis
In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

text:
[PSI-22 ACME E-FIELD Flames] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (ACME E-FIELD Flames) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME (gas-jet burner and coflow burner shared with CLD Flame)
Section: approach
The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces. The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air. In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment. An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing. The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames. Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects. High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution.

Section: objectives
The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process.
DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.

Summarized objectives include:
1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity
2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control
3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity
4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments

Section: approach
The experimental approach consists of the following components:
1) Modification of Instrumentation: TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation.
2) Aerosol Generation: Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion. The ARD was aerosolized with GN2 to create particle samples. The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags.
3) On-Orbit Testing: The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.

Section: hypothesis
The TSI P-Trak operates by condensing isopropanol around aerosol particulates that are subsequently laser counted. It was hypothesized that the P-Trak would not work in microgravity due to two potential failure modes that exist. 1) the system would clog or become obscured by isopropanol, and 2) the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device will cause an over counting of particulates.

The TSI P-Trak was modified for microgravity use via using capillary action to recycle the isopropanol. Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses:
1) that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity.
2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices.

text:
[PSI-62 BASS FGM modeling] Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography | Ground Investigation | fuel: solid (modeling) | hardware: 
Section: objectives
The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.
To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.

title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
text:
[PSI-62 BASS FGM modeling] Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography | Ground Investigation | fuel: solid (modeling) | hardware: 
Section: approach
The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders.
Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions. The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.

Section: objectives
The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Detailed objectives: 1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets. 2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion. 3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries. 4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction and soot-shell dynamics. 5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays. 6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.

Section: approach
The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, varied in pressure between 0.5 atm and 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 and 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes ensured stable temperature and pressure. A predetermined amount of fuel (based on target droplet size) was dispensed onto the support fiber for tests where the droplet is not freely deployed; after needle retraction, a dwell of at least 10 seconds let internal fluid motion subside. The ignitor was powered for 1 to 5 seconds then retracted. If the flow field was generated by translating the droplet, motion began when the ignitor retracted. Near real-time color video verified deployment, ignition and progress; chamber pressure and temperature were recorded. Steps: determine test parameters (pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, humidity); fill chamber; deploy droplet(s) controlling diameter; stabilize; ignite; track flame evolution with high-speed photography; adjust; analyze data.

Section: hypothesis
Sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion now include full Navier-Stokes gas-phase flow, but use approximations for chemistry, radiation, and gas-liquid coupling whose validity has not been confirmed with benchmark data. In microgravity, buoyancy is minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutal-capillary stresses, allowing clear observation of fundamental processes, including transitions between radiative and diffusive extinction of the flame. The goal is benchmark data on bi-component droplet combustion to validate simulations and develop new theoretical models.

Section: objectives
The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments.

Specific objectives were:
(1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
(2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points.
(3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures.
(4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions.
(5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.

Section: approach
The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions. In total 526 flames were studied.

Section: objectives
The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.

text:
[PSI-115 SAME smoke modeling] Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity | Ground Investigation (PSI grant) | fuel: smoke (modeling) | hardware: 
Section: approach
The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The final report for this investigation introduces the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration.The differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds was examined. Instantaneous scalar fields were used to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source.

Section: hypothesis
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.

Section: research impacts / earth benefits
Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012. The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

[PSI-10 ACME Flame Design] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design (ACME/Flame Design) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME spherical burner
Section: objectives
The primary objectives of this flight experiment are:
A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames.
B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames.
C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames.

Section: objectives
In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives:
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits.
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame)
text:
[PSI-21 ACME CLD Flame] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME
Section: approach
ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals. Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions. For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached. The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions. Flame temperatures in non-sooting regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry. Based on observations, modifications can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results. If the overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment.

text:
[PSI-21 ACME CLD Flame] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (ACME CLD Flame) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME
Section: research impacts / earth benefits
Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results. Momentum effects dominate most practical combustion devices, but the contribution of buoyancy forces is hard to eliminate in normal gravity. A goal of the study will be to apply sophisticated numerical tools and quantitative diagnostic techniques to the study of hydrocarbon diffusion flames in a microgravity environment. This will lead to a more detailed understanding of the interaction of convection, diffusion and chemistry under momentum-dominated conditions.

text:
[PSI-23 ACME s-Flame] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME spherical porous burner
Section: objectives
A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence):
Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates.
Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

text:
[PSI-23 ACME s-Flame] Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (ACME s-Flame) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME spherical porous burner
Section: approach
A series of experiments is proposed in which mixtures of various gaseous fuels and diluents will be issued into an oxidizing environment through a spherical porous burner and ignited to obtain, nominally, a spherical, one-dimensional stabilized flame. Synchronized measurements are to be made including spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux measurements, and system operating conditions (including reactant flow rates, ambient temperatures, pressures and acceleration levels, etc.). These data are to be used for comparisons of flame behavior and structure with detailed numerical simulations of the flames.
Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene will be used. Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and extensive studies have been conducted on its combustion chemistry. Ethylene is a typical sooty fuel and is also an important intermediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons. Diluents mixed with fuel are to include nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities, and carbon dioxide to influence flame radiation characteristics.

Section: hypothesis
The transient numerical simulation of spherical flames developed as part of this program includes detailed chemistry and transport models, especially radiation mechanisms. Each description of the flames obtained from the experiment, including measurements of aspects of the flame structure, growth or flame front velocities, and the specific test conditions where steady state flames, flame extinctions, flame front instabilities, soot suppression limits, etc., comprise a rigorous test of the detailed model. Together they provide a measure of the comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic and transport models.
The numerical simulation is also being used as a predictive tool to develop the science requirements for this experiment, especially the collection of test conditions and most aspects of the measurement systems. Due to time and g-jitter limitations, little of the planned test matrix can be adequately explored in the ground based test facilities, and the flight experiment definition will rely on the best effort in the modeling work.

title: Cool Flames Investigation (CFI)
text:
[PSI-39 CFI] Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: liquid droplets | hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)
Section: approach
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets. A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm. Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers. A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition. After ignition the wire is retracted. Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane. Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics. Flames were observed with a black-and-white camera for droplet size measurements. A UV camera was used for capturing the OH* radical emissions and flame size. Other high resolution cameras were used for monitoring and documentation. Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for analyzed flame radiation.

A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives. Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines. The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.
Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.

Section: objectives
This ground investigation sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames. The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames. The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity.

title: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets
text:
[PSI-60 SPICE analysis] Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets | Ground Investigation (PSI grant) | fuel: gaseous (analysis) | hardware: 
Section: approach
The approach was to combine image processing, experimental diagnostics, and detailed soot modeling. Raw Nikon NEF images were decoded into three color channels and analyzed using color-ratio pyrometry to extract soot temperature fields. Absolute light calibration from SPICE was then used to calculate soot volume fractions. For computational modeling, a coupled flow–species–soot system was implemented, modified to include radiation re-absorption and discrete-sectional aggregate formation. Simulations were performed for both Yale and ACME burner configurations under normal and microgravity conditions. Comparisons between experimental data and computed results guided sensitivity analyses of soot evolution parameters, including the effects of radiation, scattering, boundary conditions, and heat transfer to the burner structure.

Section: objectives
Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

Specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.

[PSI-106 SLICE] Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) | Microgravity Investigation | fuel: gaseous | hardware: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG), SPICE fan-driven flow duct with exchangeable burner tubes
Section: approach
The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions. A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images. Calibration tests for airflow velocity, soot measurement, and the fans were conducted to ensure the accuracy of the results. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments. Data was then analyzed to correlate flame structure with stability with flow dynamics and fuel properties.

Section: objectives
The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
text:
[PSI-117 Cool-flame CFD (FLEX)] Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis | Ground Investigation (PSI grant) | fuel: liquid droplets (modeling) | hardware: 
Section: approach
OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.

title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

[PSI-117 Cool-flame CFD (FLEX)] Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis | Ground Investigation (PSI grant) | fuel: liquid droplets (modeling) | hardware: 
Section: hypothesis
External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.

text:
[PSI-142 Cool-flame counterflow (FLEX)] Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames | Ground Investigation | fuel: gaseous / modeling | hardware: 
Section: objectives
By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.
5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.

Section: approach
Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures.

Specific research details are outlined in the publication, 'Dynamics of cool flames' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; 'Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and 'Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].

Section: research impacts / earth benefits
Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

Section: Summary
For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

[Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data (Challenge Details)]
Section: Background
Fire hazards are extremely dangerous in space exploration! In describing a smoke alarm that went off during the recent Artemis II mission, the commander commented, "[If] you want to get somebody's attention really quick, make the fire alarm go off in your spacecraft when you're still about 80,000 miles from home." Decades earlier, the Apollo 13 crew endured the life-threatening results of an oxygen tank explosion on their way to the Moon. Similarly, a multinational crew survived a fire aboard the Mir space station caused by an oxygen generator failure. In 1967, the Apollo 1 crew died in a pre-launch test when fire erupted in their oxygen-filled spacecraft. Compared to Earth, flames in free fall (i.e., in microgravity) are often dramatically different because of the absence of buoyancy and thus rising hot gases. Instead of a flickering teardrop, a candle flame becomes a ghostly blue sphere reliant on diffusion for its oxygen. NASA's spacecraft fire safety work is focused on prevention, detection, and suppression. Prevention is achieved by controlling ignition sources and through material selection, which depends on understanding flammability limits. To facilitate spacesuit use, an atmosphere with increased oxygen and reduced pressure compared to Earth's is expected within the planned Moon Base and pressurized rovers. Flammability is highly dependent on oxygen concentration, and air flow is also important in microgravity. Flammability studies focus on solid materials such as fabrics and plastics, as studied in the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) and Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-I, -II, and -III) investigations. Fire detection was tested in microgravity through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R).

Section: Objectives
Results from low-gravity combustion experiments, conducted for example on the International Space Station (ISS), are being made publicly available through NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database, but the amount of data can be overwhelming. It can be hard to find, harder to compare, and harder yet to interpret.

Your challenge is to build an SI-powered, web-based dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets combustion science investigations to deliver critical foundational insights for fire safety. You may consider enabling users to:

- Identify investigations most relevant to the fire safety needs of habitable crew environments, including spacecraft, space stations, bases on the lunar and Martian surfaces, and pressurized rovers.*
- Extract data that supports predictive modeling of flammability and fire scenarios in space exploration.
- Highlight research that informs the development of next-generation fire safety controls and equipment.

In this challenge, you'll help turn complex data into clear answers and make the next giant leap a safer one.

Your dashboard could also address potential applications of the PSI data to fire safety on Earth. Fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for use on the ISS have practical applications here on Earth, and NASA technology has similarly led to improvements in terrestrial smoke detection and firefighter gear, including protective clothing and air tanks.

*Fire safety involving rockets and propellants is generally beyond the scope of the research available in the PSI database. The high velocities within rocket engines render the combustion effectively independent of gravity — although a rocket's launch is of course strongly dependent on gravity.

Section: Spacesuits and oxygen concentration
- To enable flexibility, spacesuits are filled with 100% oxygen to only 4.3 psi (pounds per square inch), where the Earth's pressure at sea level is 14.7 psi.
- To avoid the bends (decompression sickness), the astronauts pre-breathe 100% oxygen to expel absorbed nitrogen.
- To reduce the pre-breathing duration and thus facilitate lunar excursions, it is expected that the Moon Base and pressurized rover(s) will be at a pressure and oxygen concentration between those in a spacesuit and the Earth's atmosphere.
- The intermediate oxygen concentration used on the Moon will likely be 30% or greater, with a corresponding pressure of 10.2 psi or less. Compared to Earth's atmosphere, that's more than a 40% increase in the oxygen concentration making materials much more flammable.
- Microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations were conducted as part of the ACME's Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). In those tests, the combustion chamber was filled with a mixture of nitrogen and a flammable gas (e.g., propane), while an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from the spherical burner creating an inside-out flame.

text:
[Combustion Science — NASA Glenn Research Center]
Section: Overview
In the United States, combustion processes contribute to about 85% of delivered energy and are an integral part in many industrial fabrication processes. Combustion produces greenhouse gases and soot, which contributes to global warming and causes significant health concerns. The Combustion Science Discipline conducts idealized experiments on the International Space Station where the removal of gravity enables researchers to study details of the combustion processes that cannot be readily studied on the ground. The Space Station environment also provides an important test-bed for studying spacecraft fire risk. Combustion occurs when fuel and oxygen react to produce carbon dioxide, water and heat. For the foreseeable future, the overwhelming majority of delivered energy in terrestrial applications will be from combustion or other chemically reacting systems. These energy uses cover the range from electric power and transportation to processes directly tied to the delivered material (e.g., glass and steel manufacture). These processes produce some of the most important environmental hazards currently facing humanity (global climate change, acid gas pollution, mercury contamination from coal, and wild-land fires). Despite being the subject of active research for over 80 years, combustion processes remain one of the most poorly controlled phenomena that have a significant impact on human health, comfort and safety. This is because the simplest combustor (e.g., kitchen stove) remains beyond our detailed numerical modeling capabilities. Typically, the combustion process involves a large number of chemical species (hundreds) and reactions (even thousands).

text:
[Combustion Science — NASA Glenn Research Center]
Section: Overview (2)
It is these species and reactions that determine flammability limits (combustor operating ranges) and pollutant emissions. Much of combustion research involves developing a comprehensive and predictive quantitative understanding of this complex process. This understanding usually occurs in smaller, bench-scale experiments that are amenable to detailed study and modeling. In these bench-scale experiments, however, buoyant forces, created by gravity and the large temperature differential between the flame and the ambient gas, dominate and frequently obscure the physical and chemical phenomena of interest, and hence, complicate analyses. In the absence of gravity, buoyancy can be suppressed, and the analyses can be reduced to much simpler one-dimensional systems. To understand the strong influence of gravity on flames, one can consider the density gradients in flames. Typical flame temperatures are on the order of 2,300 degrees Kelvin, whereas ambient temperatures are approximately 300 degrees Kelvin. This produces an eight-fold density change over the scale of a centimeter. The resultant density gradient induces a strong velocity field that dominates all but the highest flow fields. This flow field causes the flame to lift and point upward. The resultant flow instabilities cause the flicker typical of flames on Earth. By varying or eliminating the effects of gravity, we can extract fundamental data that are important for understanding combustion systems. This approach has been implemented to some extent in existing terrestrial reduced-gravity platforms, but the experimental time scales and sizes have been limited.

[Combustion Science — NASA Glenn Research Center]
Section: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction investigation (SoFIE)
Fire can be a catastrophic hazard for manned spacecraft. NASA mitigates the risk of fire with the implementation of NASA-STD-6001, which establishes program requirements for evaluation, testing, and selection of materials to preclude unsafe conditions related to flammability, odor, offgassing, and fluid compatibility. NASA-STD-6001 implements a 1-g flame propagation test for proposed space flight materials which some researchers believe is not conservative in low-g. SoFIE explores fire growth and fire safety techniques in space.

[A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (ISS, October 2015 Edition)]
Section: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (October 2015 Edition)
Authors: Suleyman A. Gokoglu (NASA Glenn), Daniel L. Dietrich (NASA Glenn), Dennis P. Stocker (NASA Glenn), Paul V. Ferkul (Universities Space Research Association), Sandy L. Olson (NASA Glenn), Michael C. Hicks (NASA Glenn).

Combustion processes remain among the most poorly controlled phenomena, yet have a significant impact on human health, comfort and safety.

Combustion occurs when fuel and oxygen react to produce carbon dioxide, water and heat. Combustion research involves developing a comprehensive and predictive quantitative understanding of this complex process. In the absence of gravity, buoyancy can be suppressed, and the analyses can be reduced to much simpler one-dimensional systems, adding to the body of knowledge.

For future exploration missions, fire safety is an important operational element to minimize the likelihood and impact of accidental fires in spacecraft and human habitats. An improved knowledge of combustion in reduced gravity is essential to adapting fire safety concepts and systems to the conditions of the space environment.

This Researcher's Guide provides an overview of combustion science research, including past research, lessons learned, opportunities for future research and introductory information on funding opportunities.

title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) — fire, investigation and lessons learned
tags: [history, mishap, fire, 100%-oxygen, Apollo, lessons-learned, materials, hatch]
text:
[Apollo 1 (AS-204) — fire, investigation and lessons learned]
Section: Mission
The Apollo 1 mission was set to be the first crewed flight of the Apollo program and was scheduled to launch on Feb. 21, 1967. It would be a 14-day Earth orbital test flight of a Block I Apollo Command and Service Module (CSM). The primary objectives included testing the spacecraft's life support systems and the main Service Propulsion System (SPS) engine. Crew: Virgil "Gus" Grissom (Commander), Edward White (Senior Pilot), Roger Chaffee (Pilot). NASA announced the crew on March 21, 1966. Construction of Command Module 012 began in Downey, California, in August 1964 (North American Aviation). The spacecraft arrived at Kennedy on Aug. 26, 1966, completed altitude chamber tests in late December 1966, and was moved to Launch Pad 34 on Jan. 3, 1967.

title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) — fire, investigation and lessons learned
tags: [history, mishap, fire, 100%-oxygen, Apollo, lessons-learned, materials, hatch]
text:
[Apollo 1 (AS-204) — fire, investigation and lessons learned]
Section: The accident
On Jan. 27, 1967, Grissom, White and Chaffee were conducting a key test on the launch pad, during which the spacecraft would switch to its own internal power. The astronauts wore spacesuits with the spacecraft's hatches closed and the cabin pressurized with 100% oxygen. During the test, a flash fire swept through the spacecraft so quickly there was no time to open the hatches. Within seconds, rising temperatures and pressure caused the Command Module pressure vessel to crack, releasing flames and smoke onto the launch pad's service structure. The astronauts attempted to open the inner hatch while the pad crew tried to open the two outer hatches. By the time the pad crew opened the hatches, the crew had already perished. U.S. Air Force pathologists concluded the astronauts died of asphyxia from carbon monoxide and other toxic gases resulting from the fire; their burns were likely survivable.

title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) — fire, investigation and lessons learned
tags: [history, mishap, fire, 100%-oxygen, Apollo, lessons-learned, materials, hatch]
text:
[Apollo 1 (AS-204) — fire, investigation and lessons learned]
Section: Investigation
On Jan. 28, 1967, Deputy NASA Administrator Robert C. Seamans established the Apollo 204 Review Board, which established 21 panels. On April 9, 1967, the board released its 3,000-page report. Although they couldn't determine a specific source of ignition, investigators found evidence of arcing in several wires near the environment control system, the area with the most severe fire damage. Because of the pure oxygen atmosphere, the fire spread quickly, causing a rapid rise in temperature and pressure that led to the rupture of the Command Module pressure vessel. This rupture generated toxic chemicals that caused the deaths of the astronauts. The three-piece hatch took 90 seconds to open under ideal conditions and was impossible to open under increased pressure. Since the test took place with an unfueled rocket, it was considered non-hazardous and not reviewed by appropriate safety organizations; there was no defined process for rescuing or treating the crew. The board determined that both technical and management lapses led to the accident; both houses of Congress held hearings.

title: Apollo 1 (AS-204) — fire, investigation and lessons learned
tags: [history, mishap, fire, 100%-oxygen, Apollo, lessons-learned, materials, hatch]
text:
[Apollo 1 (AS-204) — fire, investigation and lessons learned]
Section: Lessons learned / changes
- All subsequent Apollo crews flew aboard the Block II spacecraft (docking probe and transfer tunnel).
- The three-piece hatch was replaced with a unified hatch that could be opened from inside or outside within three seconds.
- NASA severely restricted and controlled the amount and location of combustible materials in the spacecraft, and made those changes in the Lunar Module as well.
- New spacesuits were designed using fire-resistant materials.
- Management and Safety Culture changes.
- (From the Apollo 13 page) a major redesign after Apollo 1 added increased insulation to better protect wiring, which later prevented arcing when Apollo 13's cold, condensation-covered Command Module was powered back up.
